# The Dulles International Airport Main Terminal: A Comprehensive Architectural and Operational History
## 1\. Introduction: The Monument at the Gateway
The Main Terminal at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) represents one of the most audacious and significant architectural statements of the 20th century. Conceived at the dawn of the commercial jet age, the terminal was not merely designed as a facility for processing passengers but as a monumental gateway to the United States and its capital city. Commissioned by the federal government and designed by the Finnish-American master Eero Saarinen, the structure broke decisively with the prevailing airport typologies of its era . Where contemporary terminals were becoming sprawling, finger-piered labyrinths, Saarinen proposed a single, compact pavilion—a "statick" monument that would rise from the Virginia piedmont like a temple to aviation.

The building is defined by its revolutionary structural system: a suspended catenary roof that sweeps upward, supported by a colonnade of outward-leaning concrete pylons. This form, which critics have likened to a "white Viking boat sailing the rolling meadow" or a "huge, hovering hammock," was intended to capture the dynamic "soul of the airport" while providing a dignified, monumental presence . However, the architectural purity of the Main Terminal was predicated on a radical operational concept—the Mobile Lounge—which sought to decouple the aircraft from the terminal building entirely. This decision would define the airport’s operational history, leading to decades of adaptation, expansion, and debate as the realities of mass air travel clashed with Saarinen’s elegant vision .

Today, the Main Terminal stands as a protected historic landmark, having received the American Institute of Architects (AIA) First Honor Award in 1966 and the Twenty-five Year Award in 1988 . Yet, it remains a working piece of critical infrastructure, serving millions of passengers annually within a complex that has grown to include midfield concourses, an automated underground train system, and a connection to the Washington Metro . As of 2025, the terminal finds itself at the center of a renewed national conversation regarding infrastructure modernization, with proposals emerging to replace or significantly alter the historic structure to meet 21st-century efficiency standards . This report provides an exhaustive analysis of the Dulles Main Terminal, tracing its origins, its engineering, its operational evolution, and its enduring legacy as a battleground between architectural idealism and aeronautical utility.

## 2\. The Genesis of a Jet Age Super-Airport
### 2.1 The Limits of Washington National
The impetus for Dulles International Airport lay in the rapid evolution of aviation technology following World War II. By the late 1940s, Washington National Airport (now Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport), located just across the Potomac River from the District of Columbia, was approaching its operational limits. Commissioned in 1941, National Airport was a product of the propeller era. Its runways were relatively short, its approaches were constrained by the river and the monumental core of the capital, and its terminal facilities were quickly becoming congested. As the aviation industry began to transition toward jet propulsion—heralded by the De Havilland Comet and the Boeing 707—it became clear that National Airport could not safely or efficiently accommodate the noise, runway length requirements, and fuel loads of the coming jetliners .

In 1950, Congress passed the Washington Airport Act, authorizing the construction of a second airport to serve the National Capital Region. The search for a site was exhaustive, driven by the need for a location that could accommodate the immense noise footprint of early turbojet engines without disrupting residential communities—a lesson learned from the noise complaints plaguing airports in New York and Chicago.

### 2.2 Site Selection and the Buffer Zone Concept
In 1958, after studying numerous locations, President Dwight D. Eisenhower personally selected a 10,000-acre site in Chantilly, Virginia, straddling the border of Fairfax and Loudoun Counties . At the time, this area was rural farmland, located approximately 26 miles west of downtown Washington, D.C. The sheer size of the acquisition was unprecedented; for comparison, National Airport sat on a mere 861 acres. The logic behind the massive 10,000-acre footprint (later expanded to 11,184 acres) was the creation of a "noise buffer" .

Planners graded only 3,000 acres for the actual airport operations—runways, taxiways, and the terminal complex. The remaining 7,000+ acres were retained as a greenbelt, with boundaries established at least 8,000 feet from the ends of all runways. This foresight made Dulles the first airport in the world designed specifically for the commercial jet, incorporating the acoustic realities of the jet engine into its very geography . The isolation of the site, however, necessitated the construction of a dedicated highway—the Dulles Access Road—to link the remote facility to the population center it was meant to serve .

### 2.3 The Commissioning of Eero Saarinen
Responsibility for the design and construction of the airport fell to the Civil Aeronautics Administration (CAA), the precursor to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). In May 1958, the CAA selected the New York-based engineering firm Ammann & Whitney as the prime contractor for the project. However, recognizing the symbolic importance of the terminal as the nation's primary international gateway, the CAA sought an architect capable of producing a building of monumental quality. They turned to Eero Saarinen and Associates of Hamden, Connecticut .

Eero Saarinen was, at the time, one of the most celebrated and controversial figures in modern architecture. He had recently completed the TWA Flight Center at Idlewild (now JFK) Airport in New York, a building defined by its fluid, bird-like concrete shells. While the TWA terminal was an expression of the excitement and romance of travel, Saarinen approached the Dulles commission with a different philosophical intent. He believed that the federal airport required a sense of dignity and permanence that transcended the commercial excitement of an airline-specific terminal. He sought to create a "statick" monument—a building that would anchor the landscape and provide a calm, orderly procession for the traveler .

## 3\. Architectural Design Philosophy
### 3.1 Analyzing the "Terminal Problem"
Saarinen began the design process by sending teams of architects with stopwatches to major airports across the United States. Their mission was to analyze the passenger experience, specifically the movement patterns and walking distances. The data they returned confirmed Saarinen’s suspicions: the traditional "finger" terminal design was failing .

In the finger system, a central terminal building processed passengers, who then walked down long piers (fingers) to reach their gates. As aircraft grew larger and required more frontage at the gate (for wing clearance and fueling), these fingers had to grow longer. Saarinen calculated that at large hub airports, passengers were walking thousands of feet—often carrying luggage—to reach the furthest gates. He argued that this system was fundamentally flawed for the jet age, as the scale of the aircraft was dictating an inhumane scale for the building .

### 3.2 The Mobile Lounge Solution
To solve this problem, Saarinen proposed a radical decoupling of the terminal from the aircraft. If the aircraft did not need to dock at the building, the building did not need to sprawl. He conceived of the "Mobile Lounge"—a vehicle that was part waiting room, part bus .

Under this concept, the passenger would enter the terminal, check their bags, and proceed to a gate which was, in fact, a docking port for the Mobile Lounge. They would enter the lounge, take a seat, and wait. At the appointed time, the lounge would detach from the terminal, drive across the apron, and mate directly with the aircraft parked on a remote service ramp. This system promised to reduce walking distances to a mere few hundred feet and allowed the terminal to remain a compact, single volume .

### 3.3 The Form of the Terminal
Liberated from the need to accommodate aircraft at its perimeter, Saarinen was free to design the terminal as a pure architectural object. He envisioned a structure that would rise from the flat Virginia landscape, visible from a great distance.

The resulting design is a compact, rectangular pavilion. The original 1962 structure measured 600 feet in length and approximately 150 feet in width (excluding the roof overhangs) . The building is organized on two primary levels above ground:

* **The Upper Level (Departures):** A grand, column-free hall housing ticketing counters and the Mobile Lounge docks. This space was designed to be the "grand portal," a space of Roman scale and dignity. 
* **The Lower Level (Arrivals):** Housing baggage claim and ground transportation, tucked beneath the main concourse to separate vehicular traffic flows .

The transparency of the building was paramount. Saarinen utilized vast curtain walls of glass between the structural piers, allowing departing passengers a panoramic view of the airfield and the Virginia countryside. This visual connection to the horizon was intended to orient the traveler and build anticipation for the flight .

## 4\. Engineering the Catenary: Structure as Sculpture
The defining element of the Dulles Main Terminal is its roof. Saarinen sought a form that would express the dynamics of flight without resorting to literal metaphors. He chose a suspended catenary structure, a system where the roof deck is supported by cables draped between two lines of supports.

### 4.1 The Pylons
The roof is supported by two rows of massive reinforced concrete pylons.

* **Landside Pylons:** On the north facade, facing the approaching roadway, the pylons stand 65 feet high . These monumental columns serve as the primary visual markers of the terminal entrance. 
* **Airside Pylons:** On the south facade, facing the airfield, the pylons are shorter, standing 40 feet high .

This height differential—65 feet dropping to 40 feet—creates a dynamic, asymmetrical profile. The roof swoops down from the entrance toward the airfield, physically and visually pulling the passenger toward the planes. The pylons themselves are tapered and inclined outward, leaning away from the building. This is not merely an aesthetic choice; the outward lean counteracts the immense inward pull of the suspension cables, allowing the pylons to act as dynamic structural piers .

### 4.2 The Suspension System
Spanning between these pylons are heavy steel cables, spaced at regular intervals. Precast concrete panels were laid between these cables to form the roof deck. The immense weight of the concrete roof prevents wind uplift—a common problem for lightweight suspension structures—while the catenary curve (the shape a chain takes when suspended by its ends) is the most efficient shape for a tension structure .

A unique consequence of the catenary shape is the drainage. Unlike a domed or pitched roof that sheds water to the perimeter, the Dulles roof is concave. Rainwater flows to the center of the roof, the lowest point of the curve, where it is collected in a central trough and drained through leaders located within the building's interior, effectively creating a "spine" of drainage down the center of the great hall .

### 4.3 Modular Expansion Capability
Saarinen was acutely aware that airports must grow. While he rejected the "finger" expansion method, he designed the Main Terminal to be expandable. The building was conceived as a series of structural bays—originally 15 bays in 1962\. The system allowed for the terminal to be extended longitudinally by simply adding more pylons and cables to either end. Saarinen famously noted that the terminal could be extended indefinitely without losing its architectural character, a prediction that would be tested three decades later .

## 5\. The Mobile Lounge: Innovation and Obsolescence
### 5.1 Design and Fabrication
The Mobile Lounge was a technological marvel in its own right. Saarinen collaborated with the Chrysler Corporation (Defense Operations Division) and the Budd Company to engineer these vehicles.

* **Dimensions:** Each lounge was a behemoth, weighing 76 tons and measuring 54 feet long, 16 feet wide, and 17.5 feet high . 
* **Capacity:** They were designed to carry 90 passengers (seated) or up to 102 (with standing), roughly equivalent to the passenger load of a mid-sized jet of that era . 
* **Mechanism:** The lounges sat on giant rubber tires and featured a scissor-lift mechanism that allowed the passenger cabin to be raised or lowered. This was crucial for mating with different aircraft types, which had varying door sill heights. The lounges could dock with the terminal floor, then drive to the plane and adjust their height to match the aircraft door, creating a seamless, level boarding path .

### 5.2 The "Eames" Influence
To sell this radical concept to a skeptical public and airline industry, the designers enlisted Charles and Ray Eames, the famous mid-century designers. The Eameses produced a short animated film that depicted the Mobile Lounge not as a bus, but as a luxurious anteroom to the flight. The film argued that the lounge saved the passenger the "long, lonely walk" down the terminal corridor .

### 5.3 Operational Reality
When Dulles opened, the Mobile Lounges worked as intended. They kept the terminal compact and allowed airlines to park planes cheaply on remote ramps. However, the system soon faced challenges.

* **The Jumbo Jet:** The introduction of the Boeing 747 in 1970 changed the equation. A 747 carried 350+ passengers, requiring three or four Mobile Lounge trips to deplane a single flight. This created congestion and delays on the tarmac. 
* **Connecting Traffic:** As Dulles grew into a hub, more passengers were transferring between flights rather than originating in Washington. For a connecting passenger, the Mobile Lounge system was cumbersome, requiring a trip back to the main terminal or a complex transfer on the tarmac. 
* **Public Perception:** The "luxury" wore off quickly. Passengers began to view the lounges as crowded buses. The *Architectural Forum* referred to them as "lumbering beasts," and travelers frequently complained about the delay added to their journey .

Despite these issues, the Mobile Lounges (and later "Plane Mate" variants which could lift to reach the upper decks of 747s) remained the primary method of boarding at Dulles for nearly 50 years. They are still used today for international arrivals and transport to the remote D Gates, although their dominance has been supplanted by the AeroTrain .

## 6\. Construction and Dedication (1958–1962)
The construction of the airport was a herculean earthmoving exercise. Breaking ground on September 2, 1958, crews excavated over 11 million cubic yards of earth. They demolished 580 buildings, including 300 homes, and closed 15 miles of secondary roads . To supply the concrete for the runways and the massive terminal pylons, the world's largest concrete batch plant was constructed on-site.

The terminal's construction required extreme precision. The pouring of the pylons had to be executed carefully to ensure the finish quality of the exposed concrete. The stringing of the roof cables required careful calculation of tension to ensure the roof assumed the correct curve before the concrete panels were hooked into place.

Dulles International Airport was dedicated on November 17, 1962\. The ceremony was attended by President John F. Kennedy and former President Dwight Eisenhower, underscoring the bipartisan national pride in the project. In his address, Kennedy hailed the airport as a symbol of the "aspirations of the United States" in the Cold War era, presenting a face of technological prowess and modern elegance to the world .

## 7\. The 1996 Expansion: Fulfilling the Modular Promise
For over 30 years, the Main Terminal remained at its original 600-foot length. However, by the 1990s, the airport was handling passenger volumes far in excess of its original design capacity. The ticketing and baggage areas were chronically overcrowded.

In 1996, the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA) completed a major expansion of the Main Terminal, designed by the firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM) . This expansion was a test of Saarinen's original modular concept.

* **Scope:** The project added 320 feet to both the east and west ends of the terminal, increasing its total length to 1,240 feet—more than double the original size . 
* **Fidelity:** SOM went to great lengths to ensure the new sections were indistinguishable from the old. They used the same formwork techniques for the pylons, matched the aggregate in the concrete, and continued the catenary roof line seamlessly. The glass curtain walls were extended using modern glazing technology that matched the visual appearance of the 1960s glass . 
* **Capacity:** The expansion brought the terminal's total floor area to 1.1 million square feet . It allowed for a massive expansion of the ticketing counters and baggage claim carousels, relieving the congestion that had plagued the facility.

This expansion is widely cited by preservationists as a model for how to adapt historic modern architecture. Rather than building a contrasting addition, SOM honored the "statick" nature of the original monument, effectively completing the composition Saarinen had envisioned .

## 8\. Integration of the International Arrivals Building (IAB)
While the Main Terminal handled domestic arrivals and departures, international traffic required specialized customs facilities. In 1991, the International Arrivals Building (IAB) was constructed as a satellite structure located approximately 300 feet south of the Main Terminal's west end .

Originally, passengers arriving internationally would take a Mobile Lounge from their plane directly to the IAB. After clearing customs, they would exit the building and walk or take a shuttle to the Main Terminal or ground transportation.

* **Integration:** The 1996 expansion of the Main Terminal effectively closed the gap between the main building and the IAB. The two structures were joined, allowing international passengers to exit customs and flow directly into the Main Terminal's baggage and greeter areas . 
* **2009 Expansion:** On September 22, 2009, a further expansion of the IAB opened, adding 41,400 square feet and increasing processing capacity to 2,400 passengers per hour . This facility remains the primary entry point for international travelers, housing U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

## 9\. The Z Gates: A Departure from the Lounge System
Although the Main Terminal was designed to be gate-free, operational exigencies eventually forced the attachment of aircraft directly to the building.

* **The T Gates:** For many years, a set of temporary gates known as the "T Gates" existed near the control tower. These were simple structures intended to handle overflow traffic. 
* **The Z Gates:** In 2005, the MWAA replaced the T Gates with a permanent facility known as the Z Gates. Located at the far east end of the Main Terminal's lower level, this concourse covers 20,800 square feet . 
* **Configuration:** The Z Gates (numbered Z6 through Z10) are typically configured for four or five aircraft positions . They are unique at Dulles because they are the only gates that a passenger can walk to directly from the Main Terminal ticketing area without taking a train or Mobile Lounge. They are primarily used by United Express and other regional carriers.

## 10\. The Dulles Development Program (D2) and the AeroTrain
By the turn of the millennium, it was clear that the Mobile Lounge system could not support the airport's future growth. In 2000, the MWAA launched the Dulles Development Program (D2), a multi-billion dollar capital improvement campaign . The centerpiece of D2 was the replacement of the Mobile Lounges with an automated people mover (APM) system, known as the AeroTrain.

### 10.1 The Main Terminal Train Station
To preserve the historic sightlines of the Saarinen terminal, the AeroTrain station was built deep underground.

* **Depth:** The station is located approximately 60 feet below the surface . 
* **Design:** Designed by SOM (who also did the 1996 expansion), the station spans the entire 1,600-foot length of the terminal footprint. It features a massive mezzanine level for security screening and a lower platform level for the trains . 
* **Light:** Despite its subterranean location, the station is flooded with natural light. The designers installed large pyramidal skylights in the roof of the station, which sit flush with the ground level outside the terminal (in the area between the terminal and the parking bowl). This allows daylight to penetrate deep into the underground concourse, mitigating the "basement" feel common in subway stations .

### 10.2 Operational Shift
The AeroTrain opened on January 26, 2010\. It connects the Main Terminal to Concourse A/B and Concourse C.

* **Impact:** This shifted the primary flow of passengers. Instead of waiting in the upper-level Mobile Lounge docks, passengers now proceed from ticketing down to the security mezzanines, clear security, and descend further to the train platform. 
* **Mobile Lounge Retention:** The AeroTrain does not yet connect to Concourse D. Therefore, the Mobile Lounges remain in service for passengers departing from Concourse D and for international arrivals arriving at hardstands or concourses without customs facilities. The "moon buggies" continue to shuttle across the tarmac, serving as a redundant system alongside the high-tech train .

## 11\. The Security Imperative: Adapting to Post-9/11
The terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, fundamentally changed airport architecture. Saarinen's open, fluid terminal was designed for an era when friends and family could walk passengers to the gate. It had no provision for the rigorous security screening required in the 21st century.

### 11.1 Interim Solutions
For nearly a decade after 9/11, security checkpoints were jammed into the Main Terminal's upper level, cluttering the historic hall with X-ray machines and stanchions. This destroyed the "grand portal" effect, filling the open space with congestion.

### 11.2 The Mezzanine Solution (2009)
As part of the AeroTrain project, two security mezzanines were constructed below the main ticketing level but above the train station. This allowed security screening to be moved out of the historic main hall, restoring some of the openness Saarinen intended .

### 11.3 The New Security Checkpoints (2021)
As passenger numbers continued to climb, the 2009 mezzanines proved insufficient. In November 2021, the MWAA opened two new, purpose-built security checkpoint buildings .

* **Location:** These structures were built on the west and east ends of the terminal, occupying the space above the lower-level baggage claim roadway. They are accessed from the ticketing level. 
* **Capacity:** Each checkpoint is approximately 50,000 square feet. Together, they provide 23 screening lanes (expandable to 28), vastly increasing throughput . 
* **Operational Flow:** These new checkpoints allow passengers to flow directly from ticketing into a dedicated screening environment, then descend to the AeroTrain or proceed to the Z Gates. This configuration finally removed the bulk of the security infrastructure from the center of the main hall, allowing the catenary ceiling to be viewed as a continuous, uninterrupted surface once again .

## 12\. The Silver Line: The Final Link
Since the airport's inception, planners had envisioned a rail link to downtown Washington. The original access road right-of-way included a wide median specifically reserved for a future transit line. However, it took 60 years for this vision to be realized.

### 12.1 The Debate: Underground vs. Aerial
During the planning of the Silver Line extension (Phase 2), a fierce debate erupted over the station's location.

* **The Underground Option:** Preservationists and the airport authority argued for an underground station closer to the terminal, which would preserve the view of the Saarinen building. 
* **The Aerial Option:** To save costs, project planners proposed an aerial station located in the parking bowl, visible from the terminal but separated from it. 
* **Resolution:** Cost concerns prevailed. The station was built as an aerial structure along the north edge of the parking bowl, facing the terminal .

### 12.2 The Connection
The Dulles Airport Metro Station opened on November 15, 2022 .

* **Tunnel:** To connect the station to the Main Terminal, the project utilized an existing underground pedestrian tunnel that had been built years earlier to connect Parking Garage 1\. This tunnel runs beneath the parking lot and is equipped with moving walkways . 
* **Experience:** Passengers arriving by Metro descend from the elevated station, travel through the tunnel, and emerge at the baggage claim level of the Main Terminal. While not the grand entry Saarinen might have envisioned, it finally integrates Dulles into the region's rapid transit network.

## 13\. Critical Reception and Legacy
### 13.1 Contemporary Reviews
Upon its opening in 1962, the Main Terminal was greeted with near-universal acclaim from the architectural community.

* **Wolf Von Eckardt:** The influential critic for the *Washington Post* was a staunch defender of the project. He described the terminal as "a grand portal" and "a white Viking boat sailing the rolling meadow." He praised Saarinen for creating a "truly outstanding modern building" that gave Washington a face of modernity . 
* **Ada Louise Huxtable:** The *New York Times* critic, known for her exacting standards, championed the preservation of modern landmarks. Her influence helped cement Saarinen's reputation as a master of the mid-century form, distinguishing his work from the corporate sterility that characterized much of the era's International Style . 
* **Paul Goldberger:** The Pulitzer Prize-winning critic has frequently cited Dulles as a prime example of architecture with a "soul." He has argued that the terminal's aesthetic power—its ability to uplift the spirit—justifies the operational compromises required to maintain it .

### 13.2 Historic Designations
* **AIA Honors:** The terminal received the AIA First Honor Award in 1966\. In 1988, it received the AIA Twenty-five Year Award, an honor reserved for buildings that have proved their worth over time. It shares this distinction with other Saarinen masterpieces like the Gateway Arch in St. Louis and the GM Technical Center . 
* **National Register:** The terminal was determined eligible for the National Register of Historic Places in 1978\. However, actual listing was contentious. The FAA and airport authorities frequently objected to formal designation, fearing that strict preservation rules would hamstring their ability to modify the airport for changing aviation needs .

## 14\. The 2025 Revitalization Controversy
As the airport entered the mid-2020s, the Main Terminal became the subject of a new and polarized political debate.

### 14.1 The "Terrible Airport" Critique
In late 2025, the incoming Trump administration, led by Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy, launched a public critique of Dulles. The administration characterized the airport as "incorrectly designed" and "terrible," focusing on the inefficiencies of the passenger experience .

* **The Argument:** Secretary Duffy argued that while the Saarinen building was "beautiful," it was functionally obsolete. The critique cited the long travel times from curb to gate, the reliance on the "moon-rover-like" Mobile Lounges (which cost $160 million to maintain), and the general layout which Duffy claimed forced world leaders and CEOs to endure an "inefficient airport" . 
* **The Proposal:** The Department of Transportation issued a Request for Information (RFI) seeking proposals to "replace or build on" the existing Main Terminal. The language explicitly invited developers to propose "completely new terminals," raising the specter of demolishing or radically altering the historic structure .

### 14.2 The Preservationist Counter-Argument
This proposal drew immediate fire from preservationists and architectural historians. Organizations like Docomomo US argued that the terminal is a canonical work of American art that must be preserved. They pointed to the 1996 expansion and the 2021 security additions as evidence that the building *can* evolve without being destroyed . The debate in 2025 centers on the tension between the building as a pragmatic machine for processing passengers and the building as a protected cultural symbol.

## 15\. Conclusion
The Main Terminal at Washington Dulles International Airport stands as a testament to the optimism of the Jet Age. Eero Saarinen’s vision of a "statick" monument served by mobile lounges was a bold experiment in airport planning. While the Mobile Lounge system ultimately failed to scale with the industry, the terminal building itself has proven remarkably resilient.

Through careful expansions in 1996 and 2009, the integration of the AeroTrain in 2010, and the connection to the Metro in 2022, the terminal has adapted to handle over 25 million passengers annually—far beyond its original design parameters. Its catenary roof remains one of the most recognizable silhouettes in the world of aviation, a symbol of flight captured in concrete and steel.

However, the 2025 proposals to "replace" the facility underscore the fragility of even the most celebrated architecture when faced with the relentless demands of efficiency. As Dulles approaches its 70th anniversary, the Main Terminal remains what Saarinen intended it to be: a place of transition, hovering between the earth and the sky, and now, between its history as a monument and its future as a piece of contested infrastructure.

The remaining 7,000+ acres were retained as a greenbelt, with boundaries established at least 8,000 feet from the ends of all runways.
This foresight made Dulles the first airport in the world designed specifically for the commercial jet, incorporating the acoustic realities of the jet engine into its very geography.
The isolation of the site necessitated the construction of a dedicated highway—the Dulles Access Road—to link the remote facility to the population center it was meant to serve.
Responsibility for the design and construction of the airport fell to the Civil Aeronautics Administration (CAA), the precursor to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
In May 1958, the CAA selected the New York-based engineering firm Ammann & Whitney as the prime contractor for the project.
Recognizing the symbolic importance of the terminal as the nation's primary international gateway, the CAA sought an architect capable of producing a building of monumental quality.
The CAA turned to Eero Saarinen and Associates of Hamden, Connecticut.
Eero Saarinen was, at the time, one of the most celebrated and controversial figures in modern architecture.
Eero Saarinen had recently completed the TWA Flight Center at Idlewild (now JFK) Airport in New York.
The TWA Flight Center is a building defined by its fluid, bird-like concrete shells.
While the TWA terminal was an expression of the excitement and romance of travel, Saarinen approached the Dulles commission with a different philosophical intent.
Saarinen believed that the federal airport required a sense of dignity and permanence that transcended the commercial excitement of an airline-specific terminal.
Saarinen sought to create a "statick" monument—a building that would anchor the landscape and provide a calm, orderly procession for the traveler.
Saarinen began the design process by sending teams of architects with stopwatches to major airports across the United States.
The mission of Saarinen's teams was to analyze the passenger experience, specifically the movement patterns and walking distances.
The data returned by Saarinen's teams confirmed his suspicions: the traditional "finger" terminal design was failing.
In the finger system, a central terminal building processed passengers, who then walked down long piers (fingers) to reach their gates.
As aircraft grew larger and required more frontage at the gate (for wing clearance and fueling), these fingers had to grow longer.
Saarinen calculated that at large hub airports, passengers were walking thousands of feet—often carrying luggage—to reach the furthest gates.
Saarinen argued that this system was fundamentally flawed for the jet age, as the scale of the aircraft was dictating an inhumane scale for the building.
To solve this problem, Saarinen proposed a radical decoupling of the terminal from the aircraft.
If the aircraft did not need to dock at the building, the building did not need to sprawl.
Saarinen conceived of the "Mobile Lounge"—a vehicle that was part waiting room, part bus.
Under this concept, the passenger would enter the terminal, check their bags, and proceed to a gate which was, in fact, a docking port for the Mobile Lounge.
Passengers would enter the Mobile Lounge, take a seat, and wait.
At the appointed time, the Mobile Lounge would detach from the terminal, drive across the apron, and mate directly with the aircraft parked on a remote service ramp.
This system promised to reduce walking distances to a mere few hundred feet.
This system allowed the terminal to remain a compact, single volume.
Liberated from the need to accommodate aircraft at its perimeter, Saarinen was free to design the terminal as a pure architectural object.
Saarinen envisioned a structure that would rise from the flat Virginia landscape, visible from a great distance.
The resulting design is a compact, rectangular pavilion.
The original 1962 structure measured 600 feet in length.
The original 1962 structure measured approximately 150 feet in width (excluding the roof overhangs).
The building is organized on two primary levels above ground.
The Upper Level (Departures) is a grand, column-free hall housing ticketing counters and the Mobile Lounge docks.
The Upper Level (Departures) space was designed to be the "grand portal," a space of Roman scale and dignity.
The Lower Level (Arrivals) houses baggage claim and ground transportation.
The Lower Level (Arrivals) is tucked beneath the main concourse to separate vehicular traffic flows.
The transparency of the building was paramount.
Saarinen utilized vast curtain walls of glass between the structural piers, allowing departing passengers a panoramic view of the airfield and the Virginia countryside.
This visual connection to the horizon was intended to orient the traveler and build anticipation for the flight.
The defining element of the Dulles Main Terminal is its roof.
Saarinen sought a form that would express the dynamics of flight without resorting to literal metaphors.
Saarinen chose a suspended catenary structure, a system where the roof deck is supported by cables draped between two lines of supports.
The roof is supported by two rows of massive reinforced concrete pylons.
On the north facade, facing the approaching roadway, the pylons stand 65 feet high.
These monumental columns serve as the primary visual markers of the terminal entrance.
On the south facade, facing the airfield, the pylons are shorter, standing 40 feet high.
This height differential—65 feet dropping to 40 feet—creates a dynamic, asymmetrical profile.
The roof swoops down from the entrance toward the airfield, physically and visually pulling the passenger toward the planes.
The pylons themselves are tapered and inclined outward, leaning away from the building.
The outward lean of the pylons counteracts the immense inward pull of the suspension cables, allowing the pylons to act as dynamic structural piers.
Spanning between these pylons are heavy steel cables, spaced at regular intervals.
Precast concrete panels were laid between these cables to form the roof deck.
The immense weight of the concrete roof prevents wind uplift—a common problem for lightweight suspension structures.
The catenary curve is the most efficient shape for a tension structure.
A unique consequence of the catenary shape is the drainage.
Unlike a domed or pitched roof that sheds water to the perimeter, the Dulles roof is concave.
Rainwater flows to the center of the roof, the lowest point of the curve, where it is collected in a central trough and drained through leaders located within the building's interior.
The drainage system effectively creates a "spine" of drainage down the center of the great hall.
Saarinen was acutely aware that airports must grow.
Saarinen rejected the "finger" expansion method.
Saarinen designed the Main Terminal to be expandable.
The building was conceived as a series of structural bays—originally 15 bays in 1962.
The system allowed for the terminal to be extended longitudinally by simply adding more pylons and cables to either end.
Saarinen famously noted that the terminal could be extended indefinitely without losing its architectural character, a prediction that would be tested three decades later.
The Mobile Lounge was a technological marvel in its own right.
Saarinen collaborated with the Chrysler Corporation (Defense Operations Division) and the Budd Company to engineer these vehicles.
Each lounge was a behemoth, weighing 76 tons.
Each lounge measured 54 feet long, 16 feet wide, and 17.5 feet high.
Mobile Lounges were designed to carry 90 passengers (seated) or up to 102 (with standing), roughly equivalent to the passenger load of a mid-sized jet of that era.
The lounges sat on giant rubber tires.
The lounges featured a scissor-lift mechanism that allowed the passenger cabin to be raised or lowered.
The scissor-lift mechanism was crucial for mating with different aircraft types, which had varying door sill heights.
The lounges could dock with the terminal floor, then drive to the plane and adjust their height to match the aircraft door, creating a seamless, level boarding path.
To sell this radical concept to a skeptical public and airline industry, the designers enlisted Charles and Ray Eames, the famous mid-century designers.
The Eameses produced a short animated film that depicted the Mobile Lounge not as a bus, but as a luxurious anteroom to the flight.
The film argued that the lounge saved the passenger the "long, lonely walk" down the terminal corridor.
When Dulles opened, the Mobile Lounges worked as intended.
The Mobile Lounges kept the terminal compact and allowed airlines to park planes cheaply on remote ramps.
However, the Mobile Lounge system soon faced challenges.
The introduction of the Boeing 747 in 1970 changed the equation for Mobile Lounges.
A 747 carried 350+ passengers, requiring three or four Mobile Lounge trips to deplane a single flight.
This created congestion and delays on the tarmac.
As Dulles grew into a hub, more passengers were transferring between flights rather than originating in Washington.
For a connecting passenger, the Mobile Lounge system was cumbersome, requiring a trip back to the main terminal or a complex transfer on the tarmac.
The "luxury" of Mobile Lounges wore off quickly.
Passengers began to view the Mobile Lounges as crowded buses.
The *Architectural Forum* referred to Mobile Lounges as "lumbering beasts."
Travelers frequently complained about the delay added to their journey by Mobile Lounges.
Despite these issues, the Mobile Lounges (and later "Plane Mate" variants which could lift to reach the upper decks of 747s) remained the primary method of boarding at Dulles for nearly 50 years.
Mobile Lounges are still used today for international arrivals and transport to the remote D Gates.
The dominance of Mobile Lounges has been supplanted by the AeroTrain.
The construction of the airport was a herculean earthmoving exercise.
Breaking ground on September 2, 1958, crews excavated over 11 million cubic yards of earth.
Crews demolished 580 buildings, including 300 homes, and closed 15 miles of secondary roads.
To supply the concrete for the runways and the massive terminal pylons, the world's largest concrete batch plant was constructed on-site.
The terminal's construction required extreme precision.
The pouring of the pylons had to be executed carefully to ensure the finish quality of the exposed concrete.
The stringing of the roof cables required careful calculation of tension to ensure the roof assumed the correct curve before the concrete panels were hooked into place.
Dulles International Airport was dedicated on November 17, 1962.
The dedication ceremony was attended by President John F. Kennedy and former President Dwight Eisenhower, underscoring the bipartisan national pride in the project.
In his address, Kennedy hailed the airport as a symbol of the "aspirations of the United States" in the Cold War era, presenting a face of technological prowess and modern elegance to the world.
For over 30 years, the Main Terminal remained at its original 600-foot length.
By the 1990s, the airport was handling passenger volumes far in excess of its original design capacity.
The ticketing and baggage areas were chronically overcrowded.
In 1996, the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA) completed a major expansion of the Main Terminal.
The 1996 expansion was designed by the firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM).
This expansion was a test of Saarinen's original modular concept.
The project added 320 feet to both the east and west ends of the terminal.
The expansion increased the terminal's total length to 1,240 feet—more than double the original size.
SOM went to great lengths to ensure the new sections were indistinguishable from the old.
SOM used the same formwork techniques for the pylons.
SOM matched the aggregate in the concrete.
SOM continued the catenary roof line seamlessly.
The glass curtain walls were extended using modern glazing technology that matched the visual appearance of the 1960s glass.
The 1996 expansion brought the terminal's total floor area to 1.1 million square feet.
The expansion allowed for a massive expansion of the ticketing counters and baggage claim carousels, relieving the congestion that had plagued the facility.
This expansion is widely cited by preservationists as a model for how to adapt historic modern architecture.
Rather than building a contrasting addition, SOM honored the "statick" nature of the original monument, effectively completing the composition Saarinen had envisioned.
While the Main Terminal handled domestic arrivals and departures, international traffic required specialized customs facilities.
In 1991, the International Arrivals Building (IAB) was constructed as a satellite structure located approximately 300 feet south of the Main Terminal's west end.
Originally, passengers arriving internationally would take a Mobile Lounge from their plane directly to the IAB.
After clearing customs, they would exit the building and walk or take a shuttle to the Main Terminal or ground transportation.
The 1996 expansion of the Main Terminal effectively closed the gap between the main building and the IAB.
The two structures were joined, allowing international passengers to exit customs and flow directly into the Main Terminal's baggage and greeter areas.
On September 22, 2009, a further expansion of the IAB opened.
The 2009 expansion added 41,400 square feet to the IAB.
The 2009 expansion increased processing capacity to 2,400 passengers per hour.
This facility remains the primary entry point for international travelers, housing U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
Although the Main Terminal was designed to be gate-free, operational exigencies eventually forced the attachment of aircraft directly to the building.
For many years, a set of temporary gates known as the "T Gates" existed near the control tower.
These T Gates were simple structures intended to handle overflow traffic.
In 2005, the MWAA replaced the T Gates with a permanent facility known as the Z Gates.
The Z Gates are located at the far east end of the Main Terminal's lower level.
This concourse covers 20,800 square feet.
The Z Gates (numbered Z6 through Z10) are typically configured for four or five aircraft positions.
The Z Gates are unique at Dulles because they are the only gates that a passenger can walk to directly from the Main Terminal ticketing area without taking a train or Mobile Lounge.
The Z Gates are primarily used by United Express and other regional carriers.
By the turn of the millennium, it was clear that the Mobile Lounge system could not support the airport's future growth.
In 2000, the MWAA launched the Dulles Development Program (D2), a multi-billion dollar capital improvement campaign.
The centerpiece of D2 was the replacement of the Mobile Lounges with an automated people mover (APM) system, known as the AeroTrain.
To preserve the historic sightlines of the Saarinen terminal, the AeroTrain station was built deep underground.
The AeroTrain station is located approximately 60 feet below the surface.
The AeroTrain station was designed by SOM (who also did the 1996 expansion).
The AeroTrain station spans the entire 1,600-foot length of the terminal footprint.
The AeroTrain station features a massive mezzanine level for security screening and a lower platform level for the trains.
Despite its subterranean location, the AeroTrain station is flooded with natural light.
The designers installed large pyramidal skylights in the roof of the station, which sit flush with the ground level outside the terminal (in the area between the terminal and the parking bowl).
This allows daylight to penetrate deep into the underground concourse, mitigating the "basement" feel common in subway stations.
The AeroTrain opened on January 26, 2010.
The AeroTrain connects the Main Terminal to Concourse A/B and Concourse C.
The AeroTrain shifted the primary flow of passengers.
Instead of waiting in the upper-level Mobile Lounge docks, passengers now proceed from ticketing down to the security mezzanines, clear security, and descend further to the train platform.
The AeroTrain does not yet connect to Concourse D.
Therefore, the Mobile Lounges remain in service for passengers departing from Concourse D and for international arrivals arriving at hardstands or concourses without customs facilities.
The "moon buggies" continue to shuttle across the tarmac, serving as a redundant system alongside the high-tech train.
The terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, fundamentally changed airport architecture.
Saarinen's open, fluid terminal was designed for an era when friends and family could walk passengers to the gate.
Saarinen's terminal had no provision for the rigorous security screening required in the 21st century.
For nearly a decade after 9/11, security checkpoints were jammed into the Main Terminal's upper level, cluttering the historic hall with X-ray machines and stanchions.
This destroyed the "grand portal" effect, filling the open space with congestion.
As part of the AeroTrain project, two security mezzanines were constructed below the main ticketing level but above the train station.
This allowed security screening to be moved out of the historic main hall, restoring some of the openness Saarinen intended.
As passenger numbers continued to climb, the 2009 mezzanines proved insufficient.
In November 2021, the MWAA opened two new, purpose-built security checkpoint buildings.
These structures were built on the west and east ends of the terminal, occupying the space above the lower-level baggage claim roadway.
They are accessed from the ticketing level.
Each checkpoint is approximately 50,000 square feet.
Together, the new security checkpoints provide 23 screening lanes (expandable to 28), vastly increasing throughput.
These new checkpoints allow passengers to flow directly from ticketing into a dedicated screening environment, then descend to the AeroTrain or proceed to the Z Gates.

This configuration finally removed the bulk of the security infrastructure from the center of the main hall, allowing the catenary ceiling to be viewed as a continuous, uninterrupted surface once again.
Since the airport's inception, planners had envisioned a rail link to downtown Washington.
The original access road right-of-way included a wide median specifically reserved for a future transit line.
It took 60 years for this vision to be realized.
During the planning of the Silver Line extension (Phase 2), a fierce debate erupted over the station's location.
Preservationists and the airport authority argued for an underground station closer to the terminal, which would preserve the view of the Saarinen building.
To save costs, project planners proposed an aerial station located in the parking bowl, visible from the terminal but separated from it.
Cost concerns prevailed.
The station was built as an aerial structure along the north edge of the parking bowl, facing the terminal.
The Dulles Airport Metro Station opened on November 15, 2022.
To connect the station to the Main Terminal, the project utilized an existing underground pedestrian tunnel that had been built years earlier to connect Parking Garage 1.
This tunnel runs beneath the parking lot and is equipped with moving walkways.
Passengers arriving by Metro descend from the elevated station, travel through the tunnel, and emerge at the baggage claim level of the Main Terminal.
While not the grand entry Saarinen might have envisioned, it finally integrates Dulles into the region's rapid transit network.
Upon its opening in 1962, the Main Terminal was greeted with near-universal acclaim from the architectural community.
Wolf Von Eckardt, the influential critic for the *Washington Post*, was a staunch defender of the project.
Wolf Von Eckardt described the terminal as "a grand portal" and "a white Viking boat sailing the rolling meadow."
Wolf Von Eckardt praised Saarinen for creating a "truly outstanding modern building" that gave Washington a face of modernity.
Ada Louise Huxtable, the *New York Times* critic, was known for her exacting standards.
Ada Louise Huxtable championed the preservation of modern landmarks.

Ada Louise Huxtable's influence helped cement Saarinen's reputation as a master of the mid-century form, distinguishing his work from the corporate sterility that characterized much of the era's International Style.
Paul Goldberger, the Pulitzer Prize-winning critic, has frequently cited Dulles as a prime example of architecture with a "soul."
Paul Goldberger has argued that the terminal's aesthetic power—its ability to uplift the spirit—justifies the operational compromises required to maintain it.
The terminal received the AIA First Honor Award in 1966.
In 1988, the terminal received the AIA Twenty-five Year Award, an honor reserved for buildings that have proved their worth over time.
The terminal shares this distinction with other Saarinen masterpieces like the Gateway Arch in St. Louis and the GM Technical Center.
The terminal was determined eligible for the National Register of Historic Places in 1978.
Actual listing was contentious.
The FAA and airport authorities frequently objected to formal designation, fearing that strict preservation rules would hamstring their ability to modify the airport for changing aviation needs.
As the airport entered the mid-2020s, the Main Terminal became the subject of a new and polarized political debate.
In late 2025, the incoming Trump administration, led by Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy, launched a public critique of Dulles.
The administration characterized the airport as "incorrectly designed" and "terrible," focusing on the inefficiencies of the passenger experience.
Secretary Duffy argued that while the Saarinen building was "beautiful," it was functionally obsolete.
The critique cited the long travel times from curb to gate.
The critique cited the reliance on the "moon-rover-like" Mobile Lounges (which cost $160 million to maintain).
The critique cited the general layout which Duffy claimed forced world leaders and CEOs to endure an "inefficient airport."
The Department of Transportation issued a Request for Information (RFI) seeking proposals to "replace or build on" the existing Main Terminal.
The language of the RFI explicitly invited developers to propose "completely new terminals," raising the specter of demolishing or radically altering the historic structure.
This proposal drew immediate fire from preservationists and architectural historians.
Organizations like Docomomo US argued that the terminal is a canonical work of American art that must be preserved.
They pointed to the 1996 expansion and the 2021 security additions as evidence that the building can evolve without being destroyed.
The debate in 2025 centers on the tension between the building as a pragmatic machine for processing passengers and the building as a protected cultural symbol.
The Main Terminal at Washington Dulles International Airport stands as a testament to the optimism of the Jet Age.
Eero Saarinen’s vision of a "statick" monument served by mobile lounges was a bold experiment in airport planning.
While the Mobile Lounge system ultimately failed to scale with the industry, the terminal building itself has proven remarkably resilient.

Through careful expansions in 1996 and 2009, the integration of the AeroTrain in 2010, and the connection to the Metro in 2022, the terminal has adapted to handle over 25 million passengers annually—far beyond its original design parameters.
Its catenary roof remains one of the most recognizable silhouettes in the world of aviation, a symbol of flight captured in concrete and steel.
However, the 2025 proposals to "replace" the facility underscore the fragility of even the most celebrated architecture when faced with the relentless demands of efficiency.

As Dulles approaches its 70th anniversary, the Main Terminal remains what Saarinen intended it to be: a place of transition, hovering between the earth and the sky, and now, between its history as a monument and its future as a piece of contested infrastructure.

5.title: FAA's White Elephant
5.content:
FAA’s “White Elephant” Theresa L. Kraus, FAA Historian 

On November 17, 1962, ceremonies marked the opening of FAA’s Dulles International Airport (renamed Washington Dulles International Airport in 1984). President John F. Kennedy officially dedicated the airport, named for the late Secretary of State John Foster Dulles, with former President Dwight D. Eisenhower in attendance. Other dignitaries celebrating the opening included FAA Administrator Najeeb Halaby, Mrs. John Foster Dulles, and former CIA Director Alan Dulles, brother of John Foster Dulles. The second airport owned and operated by the FAA, Dulles was the first U.S. airport specifically designed to handle jet aircraft. The opening ceremonies came after 12 long years of planning, controversy, and construction. With capacity at its limit at Washington National Airport after World War II, the CAA, Congress, and the White House began contemplating construction of a second airport to serve the region. President Truman signed Public Law 762 on September 7, 1950, which directed the Secretary of Commerce (to whom the CAA reported) "to construct, protect, operate, improve, and maintain" a second public airport for the Washington, DC, area. The act authorized appropriations not to exceed $14 million, and Congress subsequently authorized $1 million to launch the project. After considering several sites in Maryland and Virginia, the CAA decided to locate the new airport in Burke, VA. By the end of 1951, 1,046 of the required 4,570 acres had been purchased at the Burke location. When local opposition to the project developed, however, Congress refused to appropriate additional funds. From 1953-1955, CAA conducted a number of studies to determine the best alternative to the Burke site. In December 1955, following Senate hearings in July, the CAA reiterated its earlier position that the Maryland site occupied by Andrews Air Force Base would be the best location, but again recommended Burke as the next best alternative. Congress turned down a request for $34.7 million to complete the Burke project when strong opposition to that site continued at Senate hearings in July 1956. The following year, in August 1957, Congress appropriated $12.5 million for a second airport for Washington, DC, to be built on a site to be recommended by President Eisenhower. The President charged his special assistant for aviation, General Elwood “Pete” Quesada with site selection. In a report to Congress on January 16, 1958, President Eisenhower endorsed Quesada’s recommendation to build the airport at Chantilly, VA. Many local residents and many in the aviation community disagreed with the decision. They called the new airport a “white elephant,” claiming it a waste of tax payer money because no one would use the airport since it was so far from Washington, DC. Land acquisition began on January 27, 1958, after condemnation proceedings by the Department of Justice. With land acquisition and projected construction costs rising, on July 11, 1958, Congress removed the ceiling of $14 million for construction. On August 1, the U.S. Government took official possession of the original 8,200-acre Washington international airport site at Chantilly. Construction on what was eventually to become Dulles International Airport began the following month, on September 2. To clear the airport land, construction workers tore down 580 buildings, including 300 homes, closed 15 miles of secondary roads, excavated 12 million cubic yards of earth, and built the world’s largest concrete plant on site. The plant ultimately used more than 250,000 tons of sand, 600,000 tons of crushed stone, and 750,000 barrels of cement. By the end of construction, workers poured approximately 1.2 million cubic yards of Portland cement, not counting an estimated half-million square yards of asphaltic concrete for the runway shoulders. CAA’s successor organization, FAA contracted with renowned architect Eero Saarinen to design the terminal building. The design was radically different from contemporary terminals. By eliminating the “fingers” or spokes that spread out from other terminals to accommodate arriving and departing aircraft, Saarinen designed the Dulles terminal as a sleek, two-story building, 600 feet long and 150 feet wide. Saarinen referred to the terminal as “the best thing I have done.” His design won one of three "first honors" awards for architectural Terminal under construction excellence presented by the American Institute of Architects in 1966. The awards jury cited the terminal for conveying the "free and graceful movement that we associate with flight," and stated that the entire project set "a new high in architectural achievement by the Federal Government." In May 1978, the terminal was listed on the National Register of Historic Places. With no “finger” ramp areas, FAA contracted for a fleet of mobile lounges to carry passengers from the terminal to their departing planes or from arriving planes to the terminal. The mobile lounges, designed and built by the Chrysler Corporation Defense Operations Division and the Budd Company, were the largest passenger carrying vehicles ever built to be operated on rubber tires. At 54 feet long, 17 ½ feet high, and 16 feet wide, they compared in size to 8 intercity buses arranged with two side by side, two more parked to the rear of those, and four more stacked on top of each of the first four. The new airport opened for training and familiarization flights on October 1, 1962. After the formal dedication ceremony on November 17, it opened for commercial traffic on November 19. The first airlines to fly into Dulles on that day were Braniff, Delta, Eastern, Northwest, and TWA. Dulles’ original identifier was DIA. Because of passenger confusion between Dulles and the Dallas airport, including a number of people ending up at the wrong destination, FAA changed the identifier to IAD on May 22, 1968.

The **Dulles International Airport Main Terminal** is located in [Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudoun_County,_Virginia "Loudoun County, Virginia") and [Fairfax counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia") in [Dulles, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles,_Virginia "Dulles, Virginia"), United States. The original structure, 600 feet (180 m) long and 150 feet (46 m) wide, was designed by [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen") and completed in 1962 as the first terminal at [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport "Dulles International Airport"). Annexes to the west and east were completed in 1996 as part of a renovation designed by [Skidmore, Owings & Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_%26_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings & Merrill") (SOM), bringing its total length to 1,240 feet (380 m). The terminal is operated by the [Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Washington_Airports_Authority "Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority"), which operates Dulles Airport as a whole. The terminal's design is a [suspended structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspended_structure "Suspended structure") with roof panels of precast concrete suspended between cables which span the width of the building.

The Main Terminal's design includes parallel slanted [colonnades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonnade "Colonnade") on the terminal's north and south facades, interspersed with glass walls. The [landside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landside "Landside") facade to the north is taller than the [airside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airside "Airside") facade to the south; a concave roof supported by cables connects the two facades, descending toward the center. A concourse and [control tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_tower "Control tower") extend south toward the airport's [apron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_apron "Airport apron"). The interior was originally divided into two levels: an upper story for departing passengers and a lower story for arriving passengers. Saarinen's original design included [mobile lounges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_lounge "Mobile lounge") that ferried passengers directly to planes, reducing the need for long walks or [taxiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxiing "Taxiing") while increasing the airport's operational flexibility. The modern terminal includes four [airline gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gate_(airport) "Gate (airport)") known as Z gates, where aircraft could unload passengers directly. In addition, two basements contain security screening facilities and an [AeroTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AeroTrain_(Dulles_International_Airport) "AeroTrain (Dulles International Airport)") people-mover station.

The 1950 Washington Airport Act provided funding for Dulles Airport, land for which was acquired in January 1958. Saarinen was selected that May to design the terminal, construction of which began in early 1960. After several delays, the terminal was dedicated on November 17, 1962, along with the rest of the airport. Initially, Dulles Airport saw lower-than-expected usage, but increased patronage prompted the airport's original operator, the [Federal Aviation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Aviation_Administration "Federal Aviation Administration") (FAA), to contemplate an expansion in the early 1970s. [Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HOK_(firm) "HOK (firm)") (HOK) built two small annexes to the south in 1978, and further expansions and additional terminals were contemplated in the 1980s following increases in patronage. SOM designed annexes to the west and east, which began construction in October 1993 and were dedicated on September 6, 1996. Additional expansions took place in the 2000s, including the Z gates and the basements.

The structure was widely acclaimed when it was completed, particularly regarding its shape; Saarinen reportedly considered it his best work. The terminal has received numerous awards, including the [American Institute of Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Institute_of_Architects "American Institute of Architects")' [Twenty-five Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-five_Year_Award "Twenty-five Year Award"), and other terminal buildings have been compared with it. Though the Main Terminal was nominated for inclusion on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") in 1978, it was never added due to objections from the FAA.

The Main Terminal of [Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport "Dulles International Airport") is in [Dulles, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles,_Virginia "Dulles, Virginia"), United States, some 26 to 27 miles (42 to 43 km) from Washington, D.C.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._S4-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Haughland_1962-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Boston_Globe_1962-3)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-5) The airport, serving the [Washington metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_metropolitan_area "Washington metropolitan area"), straddles the border between [Loudoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudoun_County,_Virginia "Loudoun County, Virginia") and [Fairfax counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia "Fairfax County, Virginia").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-6) The terminal is placed between Dulles Airport's original north–south runways.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stroud_p._558-8) It is one of several terminal structures at Dulles Airport, along with several outlying "midfield concourses" and the International Arrivals Building,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-flydulles.com_1962-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._S5-10) all of which were developed after the original terminal.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._S5-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-11) The terminal was built to smaller dimensions than comparable terminals at other airports because it used [mobile lounges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_lounge "Mobile lounge"), which transported passengers from the terminal to planes[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-McLeod_1959-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._219-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Armstrong_1960-14) and, later, to the concourses.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schwartz_p._50-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Field_1999-16)

The original terminal was designed in a [mid-century modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-century_modern "Mid-century modern") style by [Eero Saarinen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eero_Saarinen "Eero Saarinen")[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-18) and was his only work in Virginia.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-19) Saarinen worked with structural engineering firm [Ammann & Whitney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammann_%26_Whitney "Ammann & Whitney"), mechanical engineering firm [Burns & McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burns_%26_McDonnell "Burns & McDonnell"), and airport consultant Charles Landrum.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._216-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._116-22) The Corbetta Construction Company was the main contractor,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960a-23) while Humphreys & Harding installed the finishes.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21) Other figures involved in the building's construction included lighting consultant [Richard Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Kelly_(lighting_designer) "Richard Kelly (lighting designer)") and landscape designer [Dan Kiley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Kiley "Dan Kiley").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-AF_p._82-21) The Main Terminal was intended to symbolize the [Jet Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Age "Jet Age")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Times_1960-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._117-25) and, from the outset, was designed with future expansions in mind.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-A-1988-05-26) Saarinen described his design as a "huge continuous hammock suspended between concrete trees",[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kohlmeier_1962-28) saying it represented a solution for what to put "between earth and sky".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Sehlstedt_1962a-29)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Roman_p._117-25) The western and eastern annexes were designed by [David Childs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Childs "David Childs"), Michael McCarthy, and Marilyn Taylor of [Skidmore, Owings and Merrill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skidmore,_Owings_and_Merrill "Skidmore, Owings and Merrill") (SOM) in a similar style to the original building.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Arch_p._40-30) Ammann & Whitney was also the engineer for SOM's expansion.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Arch_p._40-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._63-31)

[![Image 4: Dulles airport terminal and control tower on a sunny day](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Airport_Washington_Dulles_05.jpg/250px-Airport_Washington_Dulles_05.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Airport_Washington_Dulles_05.jpg)

View from the south (2020)

The original terminal measured 600 feet (180 m) long and 150 feet (46 m) wide.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stroud_p._558-8)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._219-13)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32)[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-33) Both ends were built with provisions for extensions measuring 300 feet (90 m) long,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Merkel_p._219-13)[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-34) for a total length of 1,200 feet (370 m).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Times_1960-24)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kenworthy_n797-27) The base of the original terminal, including vehicular ramps, was intended to support such an expansion,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ames_v927-35)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36) which was intended to have the same cross-section as the original terminal.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-37) In particular, the vehicular ramps paralleled the terminal for its entire proposed length, and Saarinen added empty openings at the terminal's base to accommodate future entrances.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36) When the annexes were eventually built in the 1990s, they were 320 feet (98 m) long,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reingold_1994-38)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Cullerton_1996-39)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-The_Times-Tribune_1996-40) giving the terminal a total length of 1,240 feet (380 m).[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41) Just west of the Main Terminal is the International Arrivals Terminal, which abuts the Main Terminal's base.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._67-36)

The vehicular drop-off and pick-up ramps are on the north, or [landside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landside "Landside"), facade of the terminal;[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Giles_1960-42) there were originally separate loading bays for taxis, private vehicles, and buses or limousines.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Ashton_1961-43) The ramps loop around a parking area nicknamed the "bowl",[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-44) while later parking garages were built away from the terminal to preserve views of the building.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Civil_Engineering_2000-45) The ramps are reached by the [Dulles Access Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_Access_Road "Dulles Access Road"), which leads east toward Washington, D.C.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kohlmeier_1962-28) The Dulles Access Road, the airport's original main approach road, was intended as a major part of the terminal's design, providing passengers views of the building as it emerged from the landscape;[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Mehaffy_p._4.8-46) it was landscaped by Kiley.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Freeman_p._63-31) Plans for a [Washington Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Metro "Washington Metro") line to serve the terminal had been considered since the 1960s,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-47) though the [Dulles International Airport station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_station "Dulles International Airport station") did not open until 2022.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-48) A 1996 expansion to the original terminal contained provisions for connections to a future Metro station.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Reid_1996-41)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-49)

Along the terminal's south or [airside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airside "Airside") facade, a concourse extends southward.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stroud_p._558-8) Initially, the southern facade had loading docks for 24 mobile lounges,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32) with 12 on either side of the south concourse.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Stroud_p._558-8) There is a 177-foot-tall (54 m)[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-51)[airport control tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_control_tower "Airport control tower") above the south concourse.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Jones_1962-32)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-52)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Rife_1968-53) The tower itself is 160 feet (49 m) tall and is topped by a [radome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radome "Radome") measuring 17 feet (5.2 m) in diameter; the tower was decommissioned in 2007 but remains in place.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Kelly_j193-54) The Main Terminal also has four gates known as the Z gates, where aircraft can load and unload passengers directly;[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-flydulles.com_1962-9) these are located along the southern facade, east of the south concourse.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Schwartz_p._52-55) South of the terminal is the airport's [apron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airport_apron "Airport apron").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dulles_International_Airport_Main_Terminal#cite_note-Hailey_1960b-56)

[![Image 5: Dulles International Airport showing the modern architecture with sweeping lines and large windows](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Dulles_Terminal_-_2.jpg/250px-Dulles_Terminal_-_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dulles_Terminal_-_2.jpg)

Exterior view of the northern (landside) colonnade of the terminal (2023)
